title: Short Stuff: John Cage's 639 Year Concert
summary: Short Stuff episode on John Cage's 639 Year Concert. The hosts introduce Cage's 4'33" (silence piece, interpreted as the ambient sounds of the environment), then cover his composition "As Slow As Possible" (ASLSP), originally titled "X Y Z PDQ" in 1985 and renamed in 1987, written for organ. In 1998 an organ symposium proposed a performance at Halberstadt Cathedral lasting 639 years, from the 1361 creation of the modern keyboard to the year 2000 millennium. The performance uses precalculated chord changes, with a change on September 5, 2020 and another on February 5, 2022, and it is scheduled to end in 2640. The hosts note the work is no longer on a human timescale, comparing it to cathedral building across generations. Sources cited include a How Stuff Works article with an interview with interpreter Rainer Nonnenbach (transcribed as Nugebauer) and Universes in Universe.

segments.title: Opening and introduction to John Cage
segments.summary: The hosts introduce John Cage and his famous 4'33" piece of silence, explaining that the silence is really the ambient sounds of the environment.

segments.title: Performances of 4'33" and Cage's view of silence
segments.summary: The hosts describe how 4'33" is performed, including a video of the German Philharmonic, and Cage's view that silence means only the absence of intended sounds.

segments.title: As Slow As Possible: origins and name
segments.summary: The hosts introduce As Slow As Possible (ASLSP), an organ piece originally titled X Y Z PDQ in 1985 and renamed in 1987, and explain it is meant to be played as slowly as the performer chooses.

segments.title: Halberstadt 639-year performance
segments.summary: A 1998 organ symposium proposed a performance of ASLSP at Halberstadt Cathedral lasting 639 years, from the 1361 creation of the modern keyboard to the year 2000 millennium, with the duration calculated in advance.

segments.title: Chord changes and the ongoing performance
segments.summary: Chord changes occurred on September 5, 2020 and February 5, 2022, timed so the piece ends in 2640. The hosts reflect that the work is beyond a human timescale, comparable to cathedral building across generations.

segments.title: Sources and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts recommend the How Stuff Works article and the Universes in Universe piece, then sign off.
